paper: Diaconu et al. 2020, J Antimicrob Chemother 75(12):3475-3479, DOI 10.1093/jac/dkaa374
verdict_context: REPLICATED (spot-check on deposited plasmid LR812026.1). Open questions are those the replication could NOT resolve from the deposited artifact alone.

open_questions.q: Does the host isolate MOL412 actually type as E. coli ST641 with serotype O108:H23, as claimed (C5), or would independent re-typing from the source isolate give a different call?
open_questions.basis: The paper's ST641/O108:H23 claim is not spot-check-verifiable because the authors deposited only the plasmid (LR812026.1); the elink query from BioSample SAMEA6863320 to the NCBI assembly database returned 0 hits, confirming no whole-genome assembly or raw reads were released under BioProject PRJEB38506. ST641 is a rare non-major-lineage ST in E. coli, so the assignment is neither implausible nor trivially confirmable without WGS.
next_steps: Contact IZSLT (Battisti/Franco/Diaconu/Carfora, corresponding authors) to request submission of raw reads or the WGS assembly under BioProject PRJEB38506.
If reads become available, run in-silico MLST (e.g. mlst or Enterobase 7-gene Achtman scheme) and serotyping (SerotypeFinder / ECTyper) and compare to the paper's ST641 / O108:H23 call.
Cross-check ST641 prevalence in EnteroBase E. coli/Shigella to contextualise whether ST641 is over- or under-represented among NDM-positive porcine isolates in Europe.

open_questions.q: Where in the host genome do the paper's claimed non-plasmid AMR genes (bla_TEM-1B, sul3) actually sit (chromosomal vs on a second plasmid), and is their genetic context consistent with independent acquisition versus co-transfer with pMOL412_FII?
open_questions.basis: Claim C6 asserts bla_TEM-1B and sul3 are carried by the isolate but neither gene was detected on the deposited pMOL412_FII plasmid by our abricate scan (consistent with the paper's implication that they are elsewhere in the isolate). Without the WGS assembly it is impossible to distinguish (a) chromosomally integrated (e.g. in an ISEcp1 transposition unit for TEM-1B), (b) a second co-resident plasmid of a different Inc group, or (c) an integrative conjugative element. This matters for AMR epidemiology because co-transfer risk differs sharply across these architectures.
next_steps: Obtain long-read WGS (or hybrid Illumina + ONT/PacBio) of MOL412 and produce a closed multi-replicon assembly.
Run plasmidfinder and MOB-suite on all non-chromosomal contigs to enumerate the full plasmid complement.
For each hit of bla_TEM-1B and sul3, extract ~10 kb flanking context and compare to known ISEcp1 / IS26 / Tn21-family cassettes to infer the mobilisation mechanism.

open_questions.q: Is pMOL412_FII (Italy, pig, 2019) genuinely a closely related descendant of pM109_FII (Myanmar, human patient) as the paper suggests (C7), or does a broader comparative-genomics scan against the current NDM-4-bearing IncFII plasmid corpus place it in a different clade?
open_questions.basis: The paper's evolutionary/epidemiological punchline is the Italy-pig / Myanmar-human relationship, but the replication explicitly deferred C7 as out of minimal-verification scope. Since 2020 the number of publicly deposited NDM-4-bearing plasmids has grown, and a One-Health story of European pig-to-human spillover would require the pMOL412_FII backbone to cluster tightly with animal-source IncFII plasmids from the same region and era, not merely with a single 2013-era Myanmar human isolate.
next_steps: Run blastn of LR812026.1 against nr/nt (and against the RefSeq Plasmid database) and rank hits by combined identity x coverage on the IncFII backbone (excluding the MRR).
Build a Mash / skani distance matrix over the top-N NDM-4-bearing IncFII plasmids and root a mid-point tree; check whether pM109_FII really is the nearest neighbour.

Separately align just the 16 kb MRR-NDM-4 region and check whether the MRR has a different phylogenetic signal from the backbone (indicative of independent MRR acquisition on a locally circulating IncFII scaffold).

open_questions.q: Does pMOL412_FII conjugate at measurable frequency into a susceptible E. coli recipient, and if so, is the transfer frequency consistent with the F-type tra locus predicted from its sequence?
open_questions.basis: The paper announces the plasmid but the deposited GenBank flat file alone cannot answer whether pMOL412_FII is actually self-transmissible under laboratory conditions. IncFII plasmids often carry a complete tra region and are conjugative, but individual isolates vary (tra can be interrupted by IS insertions in the MRR region). MOB-suite typing on the sequence would predict mobility class, but wet-lab conjugation is the ground truth and is directly relevant to how quickly NDM-4 could spread in a farm setting.
next_steps: Run MOB-suite (mob_typer) on LR812026.1 to predict conjugative vs mobilisable vs non-mobilisable status and identify the relaxase family (expected: MOB_F12).

Design a filter-mating conjugation experiment: MOL412 donor x rifampicin- or azide-resistant E. coli J53 recipient, selecting on rifampicin + meropenem (or ampicillin + azide + meropenem), and compute transfer frequency per donor.
PCR-confirm the transconjugant carries LR812026.1-specific markers (IncFII repA + bla_NDM-4) and is negative for donor chromosomal markers.

open_questions.q: Does the presence of pMOL412_FII in MOL412 impose a measurable fitness cost in the absence of antibiotic selection, and is that cost small enough to explain why NDM-4 IncFII plasmids might persist on European pig farms without ongoing carbapenem pressure (carbapenems are banned in EU food-animal production)?
open_questions.basis: The paper flags the epidemiological puzzle: carbapenems are not used in EU livestock, so a carbapenem-resistance gene appearing in a pig isolate is prima facie surprising. This is the epidemiologically important open question the paper raises but does not answer. Fitness cost in the absence of selection determines whether such plasmids can accumulate silently under co-selection (e.g. by sul1, sul3, dfrA12 selected by trimethoprim/sulfonamide use, or by class 1 integron linkage to other veterinary-relevant drugs).
next_steps: Cure pMOL412_FII from MOL412 (or use an isogenic plasmid-free MOL412 derivative) and run pairwise growth-rate competition assays in LB and in minimal media over 24-48 h to quantify relative fitness (w).
Repeat the competition under sub-inhibitory sulfamethoxazole or trimethoprim to test the co-selection hypothesis directly.

Cross-reference the class 1 integron cassette content (sul1, aadA2, dfrA12) against Italian veterinary AMU surveillance data (ESVAC / national reports) to see whether the co-selection agents are commonly used in Italian pig production during the 2018-2020 window.
